claim: HIV-1 Vpr antagonizes innate immune activation by targeting karyopherin-mediated NF-κB/IRF3 nuclear transport.
source: HIV-1 Vpr antagonizes innate immune activation by targeting karyopherin-mediated NF-κB/IRF3 nuclear transport
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the title and supported throughout the manuscript with experimental data showing Vpr inhibits nuclear transport of IRF3 and NF-κB.

claim: Both particle-associated and expressed HIV-1 Vpr antagonize the stimulatory effect of a variety of pathogen associated molecular patterns by inhibiting IRF3 and NF-κB nuclear transport.
source: Here, we show that both particle associated, and expressed HIV-1 Vpr, antagonize the stimulatory effect of a variety of pathogen associated molecular patterns by inhibiting IRF3 and NF-κB nuclear transport.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing both forms of Vpr inhibit innate immune activation.

claim: Vpr inhibits phosphorylation of IRF3 at S396, but not S386.
source: Phosphorylation of IRF3 at S396, but not S386, was also inhibited.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing differential effects on IRF3 phosphorylation sites.

claim: Vpr interacts with karyopherins to disturb their import of IRF3 and NF-κB to promote replication in macrophages.
source: We propose that, rather than promoting HIV-1 nuclear import, Vpr interacts with karyopherins to disturb their import of IRF3 and NF-κB to promote replication in macrophages.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism stated in the abstract and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing Vpr-KPNA1 interactions and competition with IRF3/NF-κB binding.

claim: Vpr rescues HIV-1 replication in human macrophages from inhibition by cGAMP in a Vpr-dependent manner.
source: Concordantly, we demonstrate Vpr-dependent rescue of HIV-1 replication in human macrophages from inhibition by cGAMP, the product of activated cGAS.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1A showing differential replication of WT vs ΔVpr HIV-1 in cGAMP-treated MDMs.

claim: HIV-1 evades innate immune sensing through encapsidated DNA synthesis.
source: HIV-1 evades innate immune sensing through encapsidated DNA synthesis and encodes accessory genes that antagonize specific antiviral effectors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about HIV-1 immune evasion mechanisms.

claim: HIV-1 encodes accessory genes that antagonize specific antiviral effectors.
source: HIV-1 evades innate immune sensing through encapsidated DNA synthesis and encodes accessory genes that antagonize specific antiviral effectors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about HIV-1, with specific examples provided in the introduction.

claim: HIV-1 Vif antagonizes APOBEC3G/H.
source: For example, HIV-1 antagonizes IFN-induced restriction factors through accessory genes encoding Vif (APOBEC3G/H), Vpu (tetherin), and Nef (tetherin/SERINC3/5) reviewed in Foster et al., 2017; Sumner et al., 2017.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 Vpu antagonizes tetherin.
source: For example, HIV-1 antagonizes IFN-induced restriction factors through accessory genes encoding Vif (APOBEC3G/H), Vpu (tetherin), and Nef (tetherin/SERINC3/5) reviewed in Foster et al., 2017; Sumner et al., 2017.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: HIV-1 Nef antagonizes tetherin and SERINC3/5.
source: For example, HIV-1 antagonizes IFN-induced restriction factors through accessory genes encoding Vif (APOBEC3G/H), Vpu (tetherin), and Nef (tetherin/SERINC3/5) reviewed in Foster et al., 2017; Sumner et al., 2017.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Vpr interacts with and manipulates DCAF1.
source: The HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr interacts with and manipulates many proteins including its cofactor DCAF1 (Zhang et al., 2001), karyopherin alpha 1 (KPNA1, importin α) (Miyatake et al., 2016), the host enzyme UNG2 (Wu et al., 2016) as well as HTLF (Lahouassa et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2019), SLX4 (Laguette et al., 2014), and CCDC137 (Zhang and Bieniasz, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous literature.

claim: Vpr interacts with karyopherin alpha 1 (KPNA1, importin α).
source: The HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr interacts with and manipulates many proteins including its cofactor DCAF1 (Zhang et al., 2001), karyopherin alpha 1 (KPNA1, importin α) (Miyatake et al., 2016), the host enzyme UNG2 (Wu et al., 2016) as well as HTLF (Lahouassa et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2019), SLX4 (Laguette et al., 2014), and CCDC137 (Zhang and Bieniasz, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous literature.

claim: Vpr interacts with the host enzyme UNG2.
source: The HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr interacts with and manipulates many proteins including its cofactor DCAF1 (Zhang et al., 2001), karyopherin alpha 1 (KPNA1, importin α) (Miyatake et al., 2016), the host enzyme UNG2 (Wu et al., 2016) as well as HTLF (Lahouassa et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2019), SLX4 (Laguette et al., 2014), and CCDC137 (Zhang and Bieniasz, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous literature.

claim: Vpr interacts with HTLF.
source: The HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr interacts with and manipulates many proteins including its cofactor DCAF1 (Zhang et al., 2001), karyopherin alpha 1 (KPNA1, importin α) (Miyatake et al., 2016), the host enzyme UNG2 (Wu et al., 2016) as well as HTLF (Lahouassa et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2019), SLX4 (Laguette et al., 2014), and CCDC137 (Zhang and Bieniasz, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous literature.

claim: Vpr interacts with SLX4.
source: The HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr interacts with and manipulates many proteins including its cofactor DCAF1 (Zhang et al., 2001), karyopherin alpha 1 (KPNA1, importin α) (Miyatake et al., 2016), the host enzyme UNG2 (Wu et al., 2016) as well as HTLF (Lahouassa et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2019), SLX4 (Laguette et al., 2014), and CCDC137 (Zhang and Bieniasz, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous literature.

claim: Vpr interacts with CCDC137.
source: The HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr interacts with and manipulates many proteins including its cofactor DCAF1 (Zhang et al., 2001), karyopherin alpha 1 (KPNA1, importin α) (Miyatake et al., 2016), the host enzyme UNG2 (Wu et al., 2016) as well as HTLF (Lahouassa et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2019), SLX4 (Laguette et al., 2014), and CCDC137 (Zhang and Bieniasz, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous literature.

claim: Vpr significantly changes infected cell protein profiles, affecting the level of hundreds of proteins in proteomic studies.
source: Indeed, Vpr has been shown to significantly change infected cell protein profiles, affecting the level of hundreds of proteins in proteomic studies, likely indirectly in most cases, consistent with manipulation of central mechanisms in cell biology (Greenwood et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from a proteomic study.

claim: Vpr has been shown to enhance NF-κB activation in some contexts.
source: Vpr has also been shown to both enhance (Liu et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013; Vermeire et al., 2016) or decrease NF-κB activation (Harman et al., 2015; Trotard et al., 2016) in different contexts and act as a cofactor for HIV-1 nuclear entry, particularly in macrophages (Vodicka et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with citation support showing context-dependent effects of Vpr on NF-κB.

claim: Vpr has been shown to decrease NF-κB activation in some contexts.
source: Vpr has also been shown to both enhance (Liu et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013; Vermeire et al., 2016) or decrease NF-κB activation (Harman et al., 2015; Trotard et al., 2016) in different contexts and act as a cofactor for HIV-1 nuclear entry, particularly in macrophages (Vodicka et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with citation support showing context-dependent effects of Vpr on NF-κB.

claim: Vpr acts as a cofactor for HIV-1 nuclear entry, particularly in macrophages.
source: Vpr has also been shown to both enhance (Liu et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013; Vermeire et al., 2016) or decrease NF-κB activation (Harman et al., 2015; Trotard et al., 2016) in different contexts and act as a cofactor for HIV-1 nuclear entry, particularly in macrophages (Vodicka et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous literature.

claim: Vpr is more important for replication in macrophages than in T cells or PBMC.
source: This is partly because the mechanisms of Vpr-dependent enhancement of HIV-1 replication are context dependent, and cell type specific, although most studies agree that Vpr is more important for replication in macrophages than in T cells or PBMC (Connor et al., 1995; Dedera et al., 1989; Fouchier et al., 1998; Hattori et al., 1990; Mashiba et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the cell-type specific importance of Vpr.

claim: Japanese encephalitis virus NS5 targets KPNA2, 3, and 4 to prevent IRF3 and NF-ĸB nuclear translocation.
source: For example, Japanese encephalitis virus NS5 targets KPNA2, 3, and 4 to prevent IRF3 and NF-ĸB nuclear translocation (Ye et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as an example of viral manipulation of karyopherins.

claim: Hantaan virus nucleocapsid protein inhibits NF-ĸB p65 translocation by targeting KPNA1, -2, and -4.
source: Hantaan virus nucleocapsid protein inhibits NF-ĸB p65 translocation by targeting KPNA1, -2, and -4 (Taylor et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as an example of viral manipulation of karyopherins.

claim: Vaccinia virus protein A55 interacts with KPNA2 to disturb its interaction with NF-ĸB.
source: Most recently, vaccinia virus protein A55 was shown to interact with KPNA2 to disturb its interaction with NF-ĸB (Pallett et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as an example of viral manipulation of karyopherins.

claim: Hepatitis C virus NS3/4A protein restricts IRF3 and NF-κB translocation by cleaving KPNB1 (importin-β).
source: Hepatitis C virus NS3/4A protein restricts IRF3 and NF-κB translocation by cleaving KPNB1 (importin-β) (Gagné et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as an example of viral manipulation of karyopherins.

claim: Vpr has been shown to interact with mouse karyopherin proteins.
source: Vpr has been shown to interact with a variety of mouse (Miyatake et al., 2016), yeast (Vodicka et al., 1998) and human karyopherin proteins including human KPNA1, 2, and 5 (Nitahara-Kasahara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous literature.

claim: Vpr has been shown to interact with yeast karyopherin proteins.
source: Vpr has been shown to interact with a variety of mouse (Miyatake et al., 2016), yeast (Vodicka et al., 1998) and human karyopherin proteins including human KPNA1, 2, and 5 (Nitahara-Kasahara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous literature.

claim: Vpr has been shown to interact with human karyopherin proteins including human KPNA1, 2, and 5.
source: Vpr has been shown to interact with a variety of mouse (Miyatake et al., 2016), yeast (Vodicka et al., 1998) and human karyopherin proteins including human KPNA1, 2, and 5 (Nitahara-Kasahara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from previous literature.

claim: The structure of a C-terminal Vpr peptide (residues 85–96) has been solved in complex with mouse importin α2.
source: Indeed, the structure of a C-terminal Vpr peptide (residues 85–96) has been solved in complex with mouse importin α2 (Miyatake et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from a structural study.

claim: Vpr inhibits innate immune activation downstream of a variety of viral and non-viral PAMPs by inhibiting nuclear transport of IRF3 and NF-ĸB by KPNA1.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Vpr inhibits innate immune activation downstream of a variety of viral and non-viral PAMPs by inhibiting nuclear transport of IRF3 and NF-ĸB by KPNA1.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Vpr interaction with KPNA1 was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: We confirm Vpr interaction with KPNA1 by co-immunoprecipitation and link Karyopherin binding and inhibition of innate immunity by showing that Vpr prevents interaction between KPNA1 and IRF3/NF-ĸB in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 7 with co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Vpr prevents interaction between KPNA1 and IRF3/NF-ĸB in vitro.
source: We confirm Vpr interaction with KPNA1 by co-immunoprecipitation and link Karyopherin binding and inhibition of innate immunity by showing that Vpr prevents interaction between KPNA1 and IRF3/NF-ĸB in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 7 with competition co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Vpr (F34I/P35N) fails to inhibit nuclear transport of IRF3 and NF-ĸB.
source: Critically, we show that Vpr (F34I/P35N) fails to inhibit nuclear transport of IRF3 and NF-ĸB, fails to antagonize innate immune sensing, and fails to interact with KPNA1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figures 5 and 6 showing the mutant's inability to inhibit transcription factor nuclear translocation.

claim: Vpr (F34I/P35N) fails to antagonize innate immune sensing.
source: Critically, we show that Vpr (F34I/P35N) fails to inhibit nuclear transport of IRF3 and NF-ĸB, fails to antagonize innate immune sensing, and fails to interact with KPNA1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 3 showing the mutant's inability to suppress IFIT1-luc induction.

claim: Vpr (F34I/P35N) fails to interact with KPNA1.
source: Critically, we show that Vpr (F34I/P35N) fails to inhibit nuclear transport of IRF3 and NF-ĸB, fails to antagonize innate immune sensing, and fails to interact with KPNA1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 7 showing reduced co-immunoprecipitation with KPNA1.

claim: Vpr mutants that do not recruit to the nuclear envelope cannot antagonize innate sensing but retain induction of cell cycle arrest.
source: We demonstrate that Vpr mutants that do not recruit to the nuclear envelope cannot antagonize innate sensing but retain induction of cell cycle arrest, genetically separating key Vpr functions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figures 3 and 4 showing differential effects of Vpr mutants on cell cycle and innate immune antagonism.

claim: Wild-type HIV-1 and HIV-1∆Vpr replicated equally well in monocyte-derived macrophages (MDM).
source: We found that wild-type HIV-1 and HIV-1∆Vpr replicated equally well in (MDM) (Figure 1A; Rasaiyaah et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A under unstimulated conditions.

claim: Wild-type HIV-1 and HIV-1 deleted for Vpr replicated equally well in activated primary human CD4+ T cells.
source: Consistent with previous studies, wild-type HIV-1, and HIV-1 deleted for Vpr replicated equally well in activated primary human CD4+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Dedera et al., 1989; Fouchier et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the presence of cGAMP, HIV-1 replication in MDM was Vpr-dependent.
source: In the presence of cGAMP, HIV-1 replication in MDM was, indeed, Vpr-dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 1A showing differential replication of WT vs ΔVpr HIV-1 in cGAMP-treated MDMs.

claim: One µg/ml cGAMP specifically suppressed HIV-1∆Vpr more potently than wild-type virus.
source: One µg/ml cGAMP specifically suppressed HIV-1∆Vpr more potently than wild-type virus and 4 µg/ml cGAMP overcame Vpr activity and suppressed replication of both wild-type and mutant viruses (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 4 µg/ml cGAMP overcame Vpr activity and suppressed replication of both wild-type and mutant viruses.
source: One µg/ml cGAMP specifically suppressed HIV-1∆Vpr more potently than wild-type virus and 4 µg/ml cGAMP overcame Vpr activity and suppressed replication of both wild-type and mutant viruses (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Vpr did not rescue HIV-1 replication from cGAMP-mediated inhibition in primary human CD4+ T cells.
source: Intriguingly, Vpr did not rescue HIV-1 replication from cGAMP-mediated inhibition in primary human CD4+ T cells, and cGAMP had only minimal effect on HIV-1 replication in Jurkat T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: cGAMP had only minimal effect on HIV-1 replication in Jurkat T cells.
source: Intriguingly, Vpr did not rescue HIV-1 replication from cGAMP-mediated inhibition in primary human CD4+ T cells, and cGAMP had only minimal effect on HIV-1 replication in Jurkat T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: THP-1 cells express cGAS and STING and have a functional DNA-sensing pathway.
source: The myeloid cell line THP-1 expresses cGAS and STING and has a functional DNA-sensing pathway (Mankan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support describing the cell line used in the study.

claim: Treatment of THP-1 IFIT-luc cells with cGAMP induced IFIT1-luc expression by two orders of magnitude.
source: Treatment of THP-1 IFIT-luc cells with cGAMP induced IFIT1-luc expression by two orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: cGAMP-induced IFIT1-luc activation was significantly suppressed by infection with VSV-G pseudotyped, genome-free, HIV-particles bearing Vpr, but not by VLP lacking Vpr.
source: This activation was significantly suppressed if cells were infected with VSV-G pseudotyped, genome-free, HIV-particles bearing Vpr (referred to here as virus-like particles or VLP), but not by VLP lacking Vpr, immediately prior to cGAMP addition (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Vpr-positive and Vpr-negative HIV-1 GFP stocks infected THP-1 cells to similar levels.
source: Strikingly, although Vpr-positive and negative HIV-1 GFP stocks infected THP-1 cells to similar levels (Figure 1D), induction of inflammatory cytokine, and ISG, CXCL10 was reduced if the HIV-1 GFP carried Vpr (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Induction of inflammatory cytokine CXCL10 was reduced if the HIV-1 GFP carried Vpr.
source: Strikingly, although Vpr-positive and negative HIV-1 GFP stocks infected THP-1 cells to similar levels (Figure 1D), induction of inflammatory cytokine, and ISG, CXCL10 was reduced if the HIV-1 GFP carried Vpr (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Genome-free, non-infectious, HIV-1 particles did not induce CXCL10 expression.
source: Genome-free, non-infectious, HIV-1 particles did not induce CXCL10 expression (Figure 1E,F), evidencing the importance of viral DNA in this response.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: CXCL10 expression was not induced after infection of THP-1 cGAS knock out cells.
source: Furthermore, CXCL10 expression was not induced after infection of THP-1 cGAS knock out cells, consistent with CXCL10 induction being cGAS-dependent (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Knock out of the RNA-sensing adaptor protein MAVS had no effect on induction of CXCL10.
source: Knock out of the RNA-sensing adaptor protein MAVS had no effect on induction of CXCL10 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Single round titer of HIV-1 GFP was not affected by cGAS or MAVS knock out.
source: Moreover, single round titer of HIV-1 GFP was not affected by cGAS or MAVS knock out, confirming that sensing activation does not impact single round infectivity of HIV-1 GFP VSV-G pseudotypes in this assay consistent with HIV-1 vector not being particularly sensitive to IFN (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Prior expression of Vpr reduced IFIT1-luc responses in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Prior expression of Vpr reduced IFIT1-luc responses in a dose-dependent manner, whereas the highest dose of empty vector had no effect, measured as a negative control (Figure 2A; infection data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Vpr expression suppressed cGAMP-mediated induction of endogenous ISG mRNA expression, measured by qRT-PCR for MxA, CXCL10, IFIT2, and viperin.
source: Vpr expression (MOI = 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) also suppressed cGAMP-mediated induction of endogenous ISG mRNA expression, measured by qRT-PCR for MxA, CXCL10, IFIT2, and viperin (Figure 2B) and inhibited cGAMP-induced CXCL10 secretion (Figure 2C; infection data to gauge MOI in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Vpr expression inhibited cGAMP-induced CXCL10 secretion.
source: Vpr expression (MOI = 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) also suppressed cGAMP-mediated induction of endogenous ISG mRNA expression, measured by qRT-PCR for MxA, CXCL10, IFIT2, and viperin (Figure 2B) and inhibited cGAMP-induced CXCL10 secretion (Figure 2C; infection data to gauge MOI in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: IFIT1-luc expression stimulated by transfection of herring testis (HT) DNA was inhibited by Vpr expression.
source: IFIT1-luc expression stimulated by transfection of herring testis (HT) DNA was also inhibited by Vpr expression, consistent with the notion that Vpr antagonizes DNA sensing (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Vpr reduced Sendai-virus-induced activation of IFIT1-luc, which is mediated by MDA5 and RIGI RNA sensing.
source: Strikingly, Vpr also reduced Sendai-virus-induced activation of IFIT1-luc, which is mediated by MDA5 and RIGI RNA sensing (Andrejeva et al., 2004; Rehwinkel et al., 2010; Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) and IFIT1-luc activation after stimulation with the TLR4 ligand LPS (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Vpr reduced IFIT1-luc activation after stimulation with the TLR4 ligand LPS.
source: Strikingly, Vpr also reduced Sendai-virus-induced activation of IFIT1-luc, which is mediated by MDA5 and RIGI RNA sensing (Andrejeva et al., 2004; Rehwinkel et al., 2010; Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) and IFIT1-luc activation after stimulation with the TLR4 ligand LPS (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Vpr R80A is defective in inducing cell cycle arrest.
source: Vpr R80A, is defective in inducing cell cycle arrest Laguette et al., 2014; Vpr Q65R fails to recruit DCAF1 and so cannot degrade target proteins Laguette et al., 2014; and Vpr F34I/P35N fails to bind cyclophilin A and does not localize to the nuclear membrane (Vodicka et al., 1998; Zander et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation support describing the Vpr mutant phenotype.

claim: Vpr Q65R fails to recruit DCAF1 and so cannot degrade target proteins.
source: Vpr R80A, is defective in inducing cell cycle arrest Laguette et al., 2014; Vpr Q65R fails to recruit DCAF1 and so cannot degrade target proteins Laguette et al., 2014; and Vpr F34I/P35N fails to bind cyclophilin A and does not localize to the nuclear membrane (Vodicka et al., 1998; Zander et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation support describing the Vpr mutant phenotype.

claim: Vpr F34I/P35N fails to bind cyclophilin A and does not localize to the nuclear membrane.
source: Vpr R80A, is defective in inducing cell cycle arrest Laguette et al., 2014; Vpr Q65R fails to recruit DCAF1 and so cannot degrade target proteins Laguette et al., 2014; and Vpr F34I/P35N fails to bind cyclophilin A and does not localize to the nuclear membrane (Vodicka et al., 1998; Zander et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation support describing the Vpr mutant phenotype.

claim: All three mutant Vprs were efficiently incorporated into HIV-1 GFP particles.
source: All three mutant Vprs were efficiently incorporated into HIV-1 GFP particles (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A by immunoblot.

claim: When delivered by viral particles, Vpr R80A effectively suppressed IFIT1-luc induction by cGAMP in THP-1 cells.
source: When delivered by viral particles, Vpr R80A effectively suppressed IFIT1-luc induction by cGAMP in THP-1 cells; however, Vpr Q65R and Vpr F34I/P35N had little if any suppressive effect (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Vpr Q65R and Vpr F34I/P35N had little if any suppressive effect on IFIT1-luc induction by cGAMP.
source: When delivered by viral particles, Vpr R80A effectively suppressed IFIT1-luc induction by cGAMP in THP-1 cells; however, Vpr Q65R and Vpr F34I/P35N had little if any suppressive effect (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: WT Vpr expression in THP-1 cells induced a significant increase of cells in G2/M phase of cell cycle.
source: As reported, WT Vpr expression in THP-1 cells induced a significant increase of cells in G2/M phase of cell cycle and Vpr R80A had no effect (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G; Laguette et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Vpr R80A had no effect on cell cycle progression.
source: As reported, WT Vpr expression in THP-1 cells induced a significant increase of cells in G2/M phase of cell cycle and Vpr R80A had no effect (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G; Laguette et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Vpr F34I/P35N induced G1/M cell cycle arrest, albeit slightly less efficiently than wild-type Vpr protein.
source: Vpr F34I/P35N, which cannot effectively suppress cGAMP-mediated IFIT1-luc/ISG expression (Figure 3B and G), also induced G1/M cell cycle arrest, albeit slightly less efficiently than wild-type Vpr protein, as previously described (Vodicka et al., 1998; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The DCAF1 Vpr-binding mutant Q65R did not inhibit cell cycle.
source: The DCAF1 Vpr-binding mutant Q65R did not inhibit cell cycle, as reported (Figure 3C; Laguette et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Depletion of DCAF1 in THP-1 cells by shRNA prevented Vpr from inhibiting cGAMP induction of IFIT1-luc.
source: Depletion of DCAF1 in THP-1 cells by shRNA prevented Vpr from inhibiting cGAMP induction of IFIT1-luc (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of wild-type Vpr, or Vpr R80A, prevented cGAMP activation of the IFIT1-luc reporter.
source: Expression of wild-type Vpr, or Vpr R80A, prevented cGAMP activation of the IFIT1-luc reporter (Figure 3F), and induction of endogenous MxA message in THP-1 cells (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Expression of wild-type Vpr, or Vpr R80A, prevented induction of endogenous MxA message in THP-1 cells.
source: Expression of wild-type Vpr, or Vpr R80A, prevented cGAMP activation of the IFIT1-luc reporter (Figure 3F), and induction of endogenous MxA message in THP-1 cells (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: FLAG-Vpr was found in the nucleus and colocalized with antibody staining the nuclear pore complex (NPC) when expressed by transient transfection in HeLa cells.
source: Concordantly, we found FLAG-Vpr in the nucleus, and colocalized with antibody staining the nuclear pore complex (NPC), when expressed by transient transfection in HeLa cells (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: The double Vpr mutant F34I/P35N, as well as Vpr Q65R, were mislocalized, as compared to wild type and R80A Vpr.
source: As previously reported for the single mutant F34I (Jacquot et al., 2007; Vodicka et al., 1998), we found that the double Vpr mutant F34I/P35N, as well as Vpr Q65R, were mislocalized, as compared to wild type and R80A Vpr.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and shown in Figures 4A, 4B, and 4C.

claim: Vpr remained associated with the nuclear rim despite effective Nup358 depletion, suggesting that Nup358 is not required for Vpr nuclear rim association.
source: Despite effective Nup358 depletion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), Vpr remained associated with the nuclear rim suggesting that Nup358 is not required for Vpr nuclear rim association (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transfection of THP-1 IFIT1-luc cells with HT DNA induced phosphorylation of STING, TBK1, and IRF3-S386.
source: As expected, transfection of THP-1 IFIT1-luc cells, with HT DNA,induced phosphorylation of STING, TBK1, and IRF3-S386 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A by immunoblot.

claim: Vpr expression for 48 hr did not impact STING, TBK1, or IRF3 protein levels, or their phosphorylation status at S386, 3 hr after DNA transfection.
source: Strikingly, Vpr expression for 48 hr did not impact STING, TBK1, or IRF3 protein levels, or their phosphorylation status, 3 hr after DNA transfection, measuring IRF3 phosphorylation at S386 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A by immunoblot.

claim: Vpr delivery by VLP reduced phosphorylation of IRF3-S396 after stimulation by either cGAMP or HT DNA in THP-1 cells.
source: We found that in this case, Vpr delivery by VLP did reduce phosphorylation of IRF3-S396 after stimulation by either cGAMP or HT DNA in THP-1 cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C by flow cytometry.

claim: VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 GFP-bearing Vpr reduced cGAMP-stimulated IRF3 nuclear translocation in a dose-dependent way, while HIV-1 lacking Vpr had no effect.
source: VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 GFP-bearing Vpr reduced cGAMP-stimulated IRF3 nuclear translocation in a dose-dependent way, while HIV-1 lacking Vpr had no effect (Figure 5D,E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Suppression of IRF3 nuclear translocation by Vpr was sensitive to Vpr mutation, with HIV-1 GFP-bearing Vpr F34I/P35N, or Vpr Q65R, failing to efficiently suppress IRF3 nuclear localization after cGAMP stimulation.
source: Importantly, in our experiments in THP-1, suppression of IRF3 nuclear translocation by Vpr was sensitive to Vpr mutation, with the same specificity as before (Compare Figures 3, 4 and 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–J). HIV-1 GFP-bearing Vpr F34I/P35N, or Vpr Q65R, failed to efficiently suppress IRF3 nuclear localization after cGAMP stimulation (Figure 5F, S5G) or after transfection of differentiated THP-1 with HT DNA (Figure 5G, S5H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: HIV-1 GFP bearing wild-type Vpr, or Vpr R80A, effectively suppressed IRF3 nuclear localization after stimulation with cGAMP or HT DNA.
source: Conversely, HIV-1 GFP bearing wild-type Vpr, or Vpr R80A, effectively suppressed IRF3 nuclear localization after stimulation with cGAMP or HT DNA (Figure 5F, G S5G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 GFP vector bearing Vpr minimally activated NF-κB-luc expression, whereas Vpr-negative HIV-1 GFP activated NF-κB-luc expression effectively.
source: VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 GFP vector bearing Vpr minimally activated NF-κB-luc expression, whereas Vpr-negative HIV-1 GFP activated NF-κB-luc expression effectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Activation of NF-κB-luc was dependent on viral genome because similar doses of HIV-1 VLP, made without genome, did not induce NF-κB-luc expression.
source: Activation was dependent on viral genome because similar doses of HIV-1 VLP, made without genome, did not induce NF-κB-luc expression (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 GFP-bearing Vpr, but not virus lacking Vpr, suppressed cGAMP-mediated activation of the NF-κB-sensitive gene IL6.
source: VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 GFP-bearing Vpr, but not virus lacking Vpr, suppressed cGAMP-mediated activation of the NF-κB-sensitive gene IL6 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: VLP bearing wild-type Vpr or Vpr R80A inhibited NF-κB p65 nuclear localization but VLP bearing Vpr F34I/P35N or Vpr Q65R did not.
source: We found Vpr inhibited NF-κB p65 nuclear localization with similar sensitivity to mutation as for IRF3: VLP bearing wild-type Vpr or Vpr R80A inhibited NF-κB p65 nuclear localization but VLP bearing Vpr F34I/P35N or Vpr Q65R did not (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Flag-Vpr expression suppressed GFP expression from a co-transfected CMV MIEP – GFP construct.
source: As expected Flag-Vpr expression suppressed GFP expression from a co-transfected CMV MIEP – GFP construct (Figure 6E) as well as several other NF-κB-sensitive constructs expressing luciferase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Vpr mutants F34I/P35N, and Vpr Q65R suppressed GFP expression much less effectively than WT Vpr, or Vpr R80A.
source: Importantly, Vpr mutants F34I/P35N, and Vpr Q65R suppressed GFP expression much less effectively than WT Vpr, or Vpr R80A, consistent with this effect being due to inhibition of NF-κB nuclear entry (Figure 6E, S6D, E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Expression of GFP from Ubiquitin C (Ub) promoter and elongation factor one alpha (EF1α) promoter constructs was minimally affected by Vpr co-transfection, but GFP expression from the CMV MIEP was reduced.
source: Expression of GFP from these constructs was minimally affected by Vpr co-transfection, but GFP expression from the CMV MIEP was reduced as before (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: CMV MIEP-GFP expression was induced by activation of NF-κB with exogenous tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), whereas Ub-GFP and EF1α-GFP were not.
source: Importantly, CMV MIEP-GFP expression was induced by activation of NF-κB with exogenous tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), whereas Ub-GFP and EF1α-GFP were not, providing further evidence that Vpr inhibition correlated with promoter sensitivity to NF-κB (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Vpr expression did not cause degradation of karyopherins KPNA1, KPNA2, KPNA3, KPNA4, KPNA5, KPNA6, or KPNB1.
source: We therefore tested whether Vpr expression caused degradation of karyopherins KPNA1, KPNA2, KPNA3, KPNA4, KPNA5, KPNA6, or KPNB1. We infected cells with Vpr encoding HIV-1 vector, extracted total protein 48 hr after infection, and detected each protein using immunoblot (Figure 7A). However, we did not detect reduced levels of any of these karyopherins.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7A by immunoblot.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of wild-type HA-Vpr co-precipitated Flag-KPNA1, and to a lesser degree Flag-KPNA2 and Flag-KPNA3, but not Flag-tagged GFP.
source: We found that immunoprecipitation of wild-type HA-Vpr co-precipitated Flag-KPNA1, as has been reported previously (Miyatake et al., 2016; Nitahara-Kasahara et al., 2007; Vodicka et al., 1998) and to a lesser degree Flag-KPNA2 and Flag-KPNA3, but not Flag-tagged GFP (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation support and shown in Figure 7B by co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: KPNA1 interacted with the Vpr F34I/P35N only very weakly, and much less than WT Vpr.
source: Importantly, KPNA1 interacted with the Vpr F34I/P35N only very weakly, and much less than WT Vpr, consistent with the mutant's reduced activity in antagonizing innate immune sensing (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C by co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: HA-IRF3 immunoprecipitated with Flag-KPNA1 and this interaction was reduced by expression of WT Vpr, but not inactive mutant Vpr F34I/P35N.
source: HA-IRF3 immunoprecipitated with Flag-KPNA1 as expected and this interaction was reduced by expression of WT Vpr, but not inactive mutant Vpr F34I/P35N (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7D by competition co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of Flag-KPNA1 co-precipitated NF-κB p65 and this was reduced by co-expression of WT Vpr, but not Vpr F34I/P35N.
source: Immunoprecipitation of Flag-KPNA1 co-precipitated NF-κB p65 and this was reduced by co-expression of WT Vpr, but not Vpr F34I/P35N (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7E by competition co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: Vpr does not directly promote HIV-1 nuclear entry, but rather prevents inhibition of nuclear entry downstream of innate immune activation.
source: Thus, we propose that Vpr does not directly promote HIV-1 nuclear entry. Rather it prevents inhibition of nuclear entry downstream of innate immune activation.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Induction of an innate response by HIV-1 lacking Vpr is expected to suppress viral nuclear entry because IFN induction of MxB in macrophages causes inhibition of HIV-1 nuclear entry.
source: Indeed, we now know that induction of an innate response by HIV-1 lacking Vpr is expected to suppress viral nuclear entry because IFN induction of MxB in macrophages causes inhibition of HIV-1 nuclear entry (Goujon et al., 2013; Kane et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation support explaining the mechanism of innate immune-mediated inhibition of HIV-1.

claim: Accidental infection of a lab worker with a Vpr-defective HIV-1 isolate resulted in delayed seroconversion, suppressed viremia, and normal T-cell counts without need for antiviral treatment.
source: Concordantly, accidental infection of a lab worker with a Vpr-defective HIV-1 isolate resulted in delayed seroconversion, suppressed viremia, and normal T-cell counts without need for antiviral treatment (Ali et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as evidence for the importance of Vpr in vivo.

claim: Wild-type infectious HIV-1 genome is not efficiently sensed by nucleic acid sensors, or degraded by cellular nucleases, because the capsid protects and sequesters genome.
source: We and others, have argued that the wild-type infectious HIV-1 genome is not efficiently sensed by nucleic acid sensors, or degraded by cellular nucleases, because the capsid protects and sequesters genome, while regulating the process of reverse transcription, during transport across a hostile cytoplasmic environment, prior to uncoating at the NPC, or in the nucleus of infected cells (Bejarano et al., 2019; Burdick et al., 2017; Francis et al., 2016; Jacques et al., 2016; Rasaiyaah et al., 2013; Schaller et al., 2011; Sumner et al., 2020; Towers and Noursadeghi, 2014; Yan et al., 2010; Zila et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with extensive citation support as an established model of HIV-1 immune evasion.

claim: HIV-1 infection has been described to induce retroelement expression.
source: HIV-1 infection has also been described to induce retroelement expression (Jones et al., 2013) consistent with a requirement for Vpr to suppress innate immune activation downstream of endogenous PAMPs.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: HIV seroconversion has been associated with a cytokine storm.
source: Furthermore, HIV seroconversion has been associated with a cytokine storm (Stacey et al., 2009) the antiviral effect of which may be mitigated by particle associated Vpr.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: HIV transmitted founder clones are particularly resistant to IFN.
source: These include a generally low HIV transmission frequency (Shaw and Hunter, 2012), the observation that HIV transmitted founder clones are particularly resistant to IFN (Iyer et al., 2017), and encode distinct Vpr amino acid signatures, as compared to chronic viruses (Rossenkhan et al., 2016), as well as the HIV transmission-associated cytokine storm itself (Stacey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: HIV transmitted founder clones encode distinct Vpr amino acid signatures, as compared to chronic viruses.
source: These include a generally low HIV transmission frequency (Shaw and Hunter, 2012), the observation that HIV transmitted founder clones are particularly resistant to IFN (Iyer et al., 2017), and encode distinct Vpr amino acid signatures, as compared to chronic viruses (Rossenkhan et al., 2016), as well as the HIV transmission-associated cytokine storm itself (Stacey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Vpr has been suggested to cause IRF3 degradation.
source: Vpr has been suggested to cause IRF3 degradation (Okumura et al., 2008), but we did not detect IRF3 degradation in THP-1 cells under conditions when gene expression and IRF3 nuclear transport were strongly suppressed (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated with citation support, but the authors' data contradicts this previous finding.

claim: Phosphorylation of IRF3 at S386 is necessary and sufficient for IRF3 activation.
source: Previous studies have suggested that phosphorylation of IRF3 at S386 is necessary and sufficient for IRF3 activation (Lin et al., 1999; Mori et al., 2004; Schirrmacher, 2015; Servant et al., 2003; Suhara et al., 2000; Yoneyama et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as previous understanding of IRF3 activation.

claim: Phosphorylation of IRF3 at S396 has been associated with enhanced association and multimerization with transcriptional coactivator CREB binding protein (CBP/p300).
source: Phosphorylation of IRF3 at S396 has been associated with enhanced association and multimerization with transcriptional coactivator CREB binding protein (CBP/p300) suggesting a later role than phosphorylation at S386 (Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Inhibition of IRF3 phosphorylation is consistent with reported inhibition of TBK1 by Vpr.
source: Inhibition of IRF3 phosphorylation is also consistent with reported inhibition of TBK1 by Vpr, although this study detected inhibition of TBK1 phosphorylation, whereas we did not (Harman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support, noting differences between studies.

claim: Vpr promoted infection in macrophages and dendritic cells, despite HIV induced formation of innate immune signaling complexes containing TBK1, IRF3, and TRAF3.
source: In that study, Vpr promoted infection in macrophages and dendritic cells, despite HIV induced formation of innate immune signaling complexes containing TBK1, IRF3, and TRAF3, visualized by immunofluorescence staining.
evidence: This is stated referring to a previous study (Harman et al., 2015).

claim: A crystal structure of Ebola Virus VP24 protein in complex with KPNA5 proposed that VP24 targets a KPNA5 NLS binding site to specifically inhibit nuclear import of phosphorylated STAT1.
source: A similar model of inhibition of KPNA target binding to manipulate nuclear import has been suggested by a crystal structure of Ebola Virus VP24 protein in complex with KPNA5. This study proposed that VP24 targets a KPNA5 NLS binding site to specifically inhibit nuclear import of phosphorylated STAT1 (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as an example of viral manipulation of karyopherins.

claim: In myeloid cells and T cells, Vpr has been reported to inhibit NF-ĸB.
source: Cell type clearly also plays a role in Vpr function. For example, in myeloid cells (Kogan et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2017), and T cells (Ayyavoo et al., 1997), Vpr has been reported to inhibit NF-ĸB.
evidence: This is stated with citation support showing cell-type specific effects.

claim: Other studies in T cells suggest NF-ĸB activation by Vpr to drive viral transcription.
source: Other studies in T cells suggest NF-ĸB activation by Vpr to drive viral transcription (Liu et al., 2014; Vermeire et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation support showing contradictory findings in the literature.

claim: Expression of diverse primate immunodeficiency virus Vprs in HEK293T cells could activate or inhibit NF-ĸB activity depending on the assay.
source: In a more recent study, Hotter and colleagues showed that expression of diverse primate immunodeficiency virus Vprs in HEK293T cells could activate or inhibit NF-ĸB activity depending on the assay (Hotter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support showing context-dependent effects.

claim: Vpr expression in HEK293T cells activated baseline, and TNFα stimulated, expression of a transfected NF-ĸB-sensitive reporter, but inhibited activation of reporter by transfected IKKβ.
source: For example, Vpr expression in HEK293T cells activated baseline, and TNFα stimulated, expression of a transfected NF-ĸB-sensitive reporter, but inhibited activation of reporter by transfected IKKβ.
evidence: This is stated referring to findings from Hotter et al., 2017.

claim: Vpr-mediated inhibition of NF-ĸB was relevant because Vpr inhibited an IFNβ reporter activated by Sendai Virus infection.
source: The authors proposed that Vpr-mediated inhibition of NF-ĸB was relevant because Vpr inhibited an IFNβ reporter activated by Sendai Virus infection, consistent with results presented herein.
evidence: This is stated referring to findings from Hotter et al., 2017 and comparing to the current study's results.

claim: Vpr inhibition of NF-ĸB transport into the nucleus to activate the MIEP likely explains suppression of expression from co-transfected CMV MIEP-driven plasmids by Vpr.
source: Our data also explain previous reports of the suppression of expression from co-transfected CMV MIEP-driven plasmids by Vpr (Liu et al., 2015b). Vpr inhibition of NF-ĸB transport into the nucleus to activate the MIEP likely explains these data, but another possibility is that transcription factor bound to cytoplasmic plasmid DNA has a role in importing plasmid into the nucleus, and it is plasmid transport that is inhibited (Mesika et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for previous findings with citation support.

claim: Inhibition of transfected plasmid driven protein expression may explain the effect of cotransfected SIV Vpr on STING and cGAS signaling reported recently.
source: This is important because inhibition of transfected plasmid driven protein expression may explain the effect of cotransfected SIV Vpr on STING and cGAS signaling reported recently (Su et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as a potential explanation for previous findings.

claim: Manipulation of cell cycle by Vpr is independent of interaction with karyopherin proteins.
source: Importantly, our data are consistent with reports that manipulation of cell cycle by Vpr is independent of interaction with karyopherin proteins.
evidence: This is stated based on the experimental findings showing Vpr R80A does not affect cell cycle but retains innate immune antagonism.

claim: The Vpr R80A mutant, which does not arrest cell cycle, or manipulate SLX4 complex, was functional in inhibition of innate sensing.
source: The Vpr R80A mutant, which does not arrest cell cycle, or manipulate SLX4 complex (Gaynor and Chen, 2001; Laguette et al., 2014) was functional in inhibition of innate sensing (Figures 3, 5 and 6).
evidence: This is stated with citation support and demonstrated in multiple figures.

claim: SLX4 interaction does not play a role in the innate immune antagonism shown in this study.
source: Thus we assume that SLX4 interaction does not play a role in the innate immune antagonism shown herein.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the Vpr R80A mutant data.

claim: Vpr has been shown to bind FxFG motif in p6 of Gag during virion incorporation.
source: Given that Vpr has been shown to bind FxFG motif in p6 of Gag during virion incorporation (Zhu et al., 2004), and FG motifs at the NPC (Fouchier et al., 1998) it is possible that interaction of Vpr with nuclear pore proteins via the FG motifs contribute to Vpr-mediated inhibition of IRF3 and NF-ĸB nuclear import.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Vpr has been shown to bind FG motifs at the NPC.
source: Given that Vpr has been shown to bind FxFG motif in p6 of Gag during virion incorporation (Zhu et al., 2004), and FG motifs at the NPC (Fouchier et al., 1998) it is possible that interaction of Vpr with nuclear pore proteins via the FG motifs contribute to Vpr-mediated inhibition of IRF3 and NF-ĸB nuclear import.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Replication in activated primary CD4+ T cells was independent of Vpr in the presence and absence of cGAMP.
source: Replication in activated primary CD4+ T cells was, in our hands, independent of Vpr in the presence and absence of cGAMP, which was inhibitory, suggesting that Vpr cannot overcome signaling downstream of cGAMP in these cells.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: Activated T-cells respond differently to cGAMP than macrophages.
source: This implies that activated T-cells respond differently to cGAMP than macrophages, consistent with observations that in T cell/macrophage mixed cultures, the negative effects of cGAMP on HIV-1 replication were principally mediated via macrophages (Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Vpr-sensitive, cGAS-dependent, IFN production from T cells has been reported.
source: Vpr-sensitive, cGAS-dependent, IFN production from T cells has been reported suggesting that in the right circumstances, T cells can sense HIV-1 DNA, via cGAS, in T cells (Vermeire et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 (∆Env, ∆Nef, ∆Vpr) failed to activate sensing in a variety of cell lines.
source: For example, Cingoz et al reported failure of VSV-G pseudotyped HIV-1 (∆Env, ∆Nef, ∆Vpr) to activate sensing in a variety of cell lines (Cingöz and Goff, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Other studies have demonstrated sensing of wild-type HIV-1 DNA by cGAS.
source: However, other studies have demonstrated sensing of wild-type HIV-1 DNA by cGAS (Gao et al., 2013; Lahaye et al., 2013), and here we observed cGAS-dependent, Vpr-sensitive, induction of CXCL10 or NF-ĸB reporter by high dose (MOI 1–3) VSV-G pseudotyped single round HIV-1 GFP vector in THP-1 cells (Figures 1 and 6).
evidence: This is stated with citation support and demonstrated in the current study's data.
